clinicalPearls: Botryomycosis is a rare chronic suppurative bacterial infection that forms grains resembling those of true fungal mycetoma, hence the term bacterial pseudomycosis
It is most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, but Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other bacteria are also implicated
Cutaneous disease is the commonest form, presenting as chronic nodules, abscesses and discharging sinuses, frequently following trauma or a retained foreign body
Visceral botryomycosis, particularly of the lungs, is less common and tends to occur in immunocompromised or debilitated hosts
Discharging sinuses may extrude visible granules composed of bacterial colonies surrounded by an eosinophilic matrix
Diagnosis rests on histology showing bacterial grains with the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon, together with culture to identify the causative organism
Treatment combines prolonged organism-directed antibiotics with surgical debridement or excision of affected tissue
reference.pathophysiology: Botryomycosis develops when common pyogenic bacteria establish a chronic, walled-off infection rather than being cleared, often in the setting of local trauma, a foreign body or impaired host defences. The bacteria aggregate into grains encased in an eosinophilic, immunoglobulin-rich matrix (the Splendore-Hoeppli reaction), which shields them from immune attack and antibiotics. Surrounding chronic suppurative and granulomatous inflammation produces nodules, abscesses and sinus tracts, closely mimicking the clinical and histological picture of fungal or actinomycotic mycetoma despite being purely bacterial in origin.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic bacterial osteomyelitis with sinus formation
Cutaneous tuberculosis or atypical mycobacterial infection
Deep fungal infection such as sporotrichosis or chromoblastomycosis
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy for histology showing bacterial grains and the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon
Gram stain and culture of grains and tissue to identify the causative bacterium
Special stains to distinguish bacterial grains from fungal and actinomycotic ones
Imaging to assess deep tissue, bone or visceral involvement
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing to direct prolonged therapy
Assessment of immune status and search for a retained foreign body
redFlags: Visceral or pulmonary involvement in an immunocompromised patient
Extension of infection into bone or deep structures
Non-healing sinuses despite standard antibiotic courses
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring exclusion of mycetoma or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Localised cutaneous disease usually responds well to prolonged antibiotics combined with surgical excision, whereas visceral disease in compromised hosts is more difficult to eradicate and carries a poorer outcome.
pitfalls: Mistaking bacterial grains for fungal mycetoma and giving inappropriate antifungal therapy
Relying on antibiotics alone without surgical removal of affected tissue or foreign body
Truncating therapy before the chronic infection is fully cleared
Overlooking underlying immunosuppression in visceral disease
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Prolonged culture-directed antibacterial therapy, typically antistaphylococcal agents for Staphylococcus aureus and antipseudomonal cover when Pseudomonas aeruginosa is implicated
Surgical debridement or excision of nodules, abscesses and discharging sinus tracts to remove the protective grain matrix that shields bacteria from antibiotics
Removal of any retained foreign body that is sustaining the walled-off infection
Extended treatment course continued until clinical and radiological resolution, given the difficulty eradicating grain-encased organisms
Assessment and optimisation of host immune status and any underlying debilitation
Imaging surveillance for deep soft-tissue, bony or visceral (particularly pulmonary) extension
Combined infectious diseases and surgical input to guide antimicrobial choice and source control
